title: Who keeps the UK connected? Communications, cyber and public resilience
label: 11 June 2026 · National Resilience Committee
summary: Witnesses from Bournemouth University and Ofcom told the committee that public awareness of national and international risks is low and locally focused, that communicating resilience needs tailored, well‑resourced campaigns, and that telecoms and cyber resilience require continuous cross‑sector work, practical redundancy and trust-building. They warned that switching off terrestrial TV or assuming universal digital access would create gaps unless replacements are proven resilient, and recommended clearer whole‑society plans and greater trust in institutions.

chapters.title: How aware is the public?
chapters.takeaway: Public awareness of national and interconnected risks is generally low and focused on immediate local threats.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: To start: how aware is the public of connected national and international risks, including those tied to communications?

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: Ofcom mostly talks to the industry we regulate, not the public directly, but we do publish consumer guidance and sector risk reports like Connected Nations to raise awareness.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You said you monitor industry compliance—how compliant is industry?

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: Telecoms are following a journey under the Telecommunications (Security) Act. Operators are taking steps to meet requirements, but threats evolve so it’s ongoing.

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: From the public’s side, awareness is low. In our 2025 UK household study, only about half recognised hazards and many took no action—21% saw no risks at all.

turns.speaker: Lord Oates
turns.text: Are those household perceptions accurate—do they match real risks?

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: Perception, preparedness and outcomes differ. People focus on local, personal risks—home accidents topped the list—so national threats can seem distant and get little action.

chapters.title: Getting the message across
chapters.takeaway: Resilience communications must translate national risks into everyday choices, use many platforms, and be well resourced.

turns.speaker: Baroness Northover
turns.text: With a fragmented media landscape and young people using social platforms, how do we communicate resilience effectively?

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: Treat people as rational: they prioritise local risks. I suggest the 'four Es'—enlighten (explain why resilience matters), empower choices, enable action (incentives/support), and evaluate outcomes.

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: Use a hub-and-spoke model: a central agreed message (hub) tailored and delivered on many platforms (spokes) from TikTok to local groups. That’s not cheap—it needs resources.

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: Ofcom does consumer research, such as Media Nations; I can share that to help understand where people actually get information.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hunter of Auchenreoch
turns.text: What international examples could the UK use—Nordic countries, Africa, Caribbean?

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: Nordic countries benefit from high trust and a total defence tradition, so simple tools like crisis leaflets work there. But the UK has different social trust levels, so we must adapt, not copy.

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: In parts of Africa and the Caribbean, low‑tech redundancy—community hailer systems, local plans—matter because high‑tech backup isn’t available; the UK should keep low‑tech redundancy for rural or cut‑off areas.

chapters.title: If the networks fail: blackouts, satellites and cyber
chapters.takeaway: Planning must assume prolonged outages; telecoms and energy must coordinate, and laws and exercises are improving resilience but must stay agile.

turns.speaker: Lord Farmer
turns.text: If there was a multi-day communications blackout, and DTT is switched off in future, how would we warn the public or restore services?

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: Operators are expected to avoid single points of failure: build redundancy, test business continuity plans, and have power backups. In an outage they can deploy mobile cell sites and generators; government has satellite options and the Emergency Services Network for critical users.

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: Restoration depends on co‑operation with the energy sector to get power to sites quickly. Some communities already use satellite terminals for local resilience.

turns.speaker: Lord Farmer
turns.text: If satellites themselves were attacked or disabled, how resilient are we?

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: It’s layered: fixed, mobile, satellite—when gaps exceed commercial capacity, national arrangements led by the Cabinet Office and DSIT come into play.

turns.speaker: Baroness Mobarik
turns.text: How much of emergency communications depends on commercial networks and satellites, and what sovereign options exist?

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: I can provide exact figures later. Sovereignty is debated—trusted partners versus fully domestic systems. The UK is building layers of resilience and partnerships to reduce single‑country reliance.

turns.speaker: Baroness Curran
turns.text: Has Ofcom taken part in war‑scale contingency planning and exercises?

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: Yes—we work with DSIT, Cabinet Office and industry on cross‑sector scenarios and exercises and attend those national conversations.

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: Two points: how long an outage lasts matters—Caribbean examples show weeks without comms and months without power. Second, public expectations: many treat internet as essential, so expectation management is vital.

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: Also remember most recovery work is done by private companies; the arrangements and costs for long recovery matter beyond short MoUs.

turns.speaker: Lord Peach
turns.text: On cybersecurity: is the Government right to be proud? Are national exercises frequent and tough enough?

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: The Telecommunications (Security) Act (2021) came from NCSC threat work and gives a proportionate framework. Ofcom monitors compliance, and the government is updating the code of practice. For infrastructure beyond telecoms, the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill aims to set baselines and include data centres.

turns.speaker: Baroness Winterton of Doncaster
turns.text: Why bring data centres into legislation and what will the new Bill add?

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: Data centres are designated critical infrastructure; they underpin AI and many services. The Bill aims for oversight, better incident reporting, and attention to supply‑chain risks; details will be in secondary legislation.

turns.speaker: Baroness Mobarik
turns.text: SMEs face rising attacks—does Ofcom focus on them?

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: The code targets larger operators (turnover thresholds) but we engage smaller providers, share guidance and hold roundtables. NCSC publishes practical advice for smaller firms.

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: Codes must be agile: AI is changing attacks rapidly. Many SMEs report cyber incidents; training, simulations and educating senior management on strategic investment are urgent.

turns.speaker: Baroness Winterton of Doncaster
turns.text: Is there risk of delay while secondary legislation and training wait to be finalised?

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: We already apply the Cyber Assessment Framework in practice. Putting it in law strengthens it, but the standards are already being used—work isn’t waiting for the Bill to start.

chapters.title: Education, TV switch‑off and final recommendations
chapters.takeaway: Schools and FE/HE must teach resilience; removing terrestrial TV needs clear resilient replacements; prime recommendations are whole‑society coordination and rebuilding public trust.

turns.speaker: Lord Oates
turns.text: What role should education play at all levels in resilience?

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: Education is essential: schools can teach everyday resilience and citizenship, FE can provide practical skills and access courses, and universities provide specialist training, research and the planners of the future.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Is switching off digital terrestrial TV sensible given some groups rely on it?

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: Switching it off risks losing a universal resilience channel. If we remove it, we must clearly and convincingly replace it with services that work for older, rural or digitally excluded people and prove the replacements are resilient 24/7.

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: Technology evolves, so change may be sensible, but governments must guarantee resilience where needed and target extra protections for communities that would be disadvantaged.

turns.speaker: Baroness Helic
turns.text: If you could give one recommendation to government, what would it be?

turns.speaker: Nihal Newman
turns.text: Make the 'whole‑society' approach real: bring government, industry, communities, and academia together around clear plans and shared responsibilities.

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: Focus on rebuilding public trust. A whole‑society approach only works if people trust institutions and messages—invest in everyday resilience that households understand and trust.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you both—this highlights communications, cross‑sector working and trust as central to national resilience.
